title: The Cheapest Order to Multiply a Chain of Matrices

concept.title: Choose the last multiplication: it splits the chain into two independent chains
body: To multiply a chain of matrices `A1 * A2 * ... * An` you may put the brackets in any way, because the product does not depend on it. But the **cost** does: multiplying a matrix of size `p x q` by a matrix of size `q x r` takes `p * q * r` scalar multiplications. For the sizes `10x30`, `30x5`, `5x60` the order `(A1 A2) A3` costs 10*30*5 + 10*5*60 = 4500, and `A1 (A2 A3)` costs 30*5*60 + 10*30*60 = 27000. Find the smallest total cost over all the ways to put brackets.

Describe the matrices by the list of dimensions `d`: the matrix `i` has `d[i]` rows and `d[i + 1]` columns, so neighbours always fit. Let `cost(i, j)` be the smallest cost to multiply the matrices `i .. j` (`cost(i, i) = 0`). In an optimal bracketing the **last multiplication** joins the product of `i .. k` with the product of `k + 1 .. j`; the two parts are independent, and the last product multiplies a `d[i] x d[k+1]` matrix by a `d[k+1] x d[j+1]` matrix: **`cost(i, j) = min over k of cost(i, k) + cost(k + 1, j) + d[i] * d[k + 1] * d[j + 1]`**.

The chains are processed from short to long. There are O(n^2) chains and O(n) split points: O(n^3) time and O(n^2) memory. The same table shape solves "optimal way to evaluate an expression", "optimal triangulation of a polygon" and many other interval problems where a final operation joins two independent parts.

statement: A chain of `n = m - 1` matrices is given by the list of `m` dimensions: the matrix `i` has `d[i]` rows and `d[i + 1]` columns. Multiplying a `p x q` matrix by a `q x r` matrix costs `p * q * r`. Print the smallest total cost of multiplying the whole chain, over all ways to place the brackets.
inputFormat: The first line has `m`: the number of dimensions (so there are `m - 1` matrices).
The second line has `m` numbers: the matrix number `i` has `d[i]` rows and `d[i + 1]` columns.

examples.note: Multiply (A1 A2) first: 10*30*5 = 1500, then by A3: 10*5*60 = 3000. Total 4500.
A single matrix needs no multiplication: 0.

hints: Let cost(i, j) be the smallest cost for the matrices i to j; cost(i, i) = 0.
Try every split k: cost(i, k) + cost(k + 1, j) + d[i] * d[k + 1] * d[j + 1].
Fill the table by increasing chain length.

import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

m = int(input())

# Your code here

explanation: cost(i, j), the smallest cost to multiply the matrices i to j, is the minimum over the split k of cost(i, k) + cost(k + 1, j) + d[i] * d[k + 1] * d[j + 1], with cost(i, i) = 0; the table is filled by increasing chain length.

code.python:
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

m = int(input())
d = list(map(int, input().split()))

n = m - 1
cost = [[0] * n for _ in range(n)]
for length in range(2, n + 1):
    for i in range(n - length + 1):
        j = i + length - 1
        best = None
        di = d[i]
        dj = d[j + 1]
        for k in range(i, j):
            v = cost[i][k] + cost[k + 1][j] + di * d[k + 1] * dj
            if best is None or v < best:
                best = v
        cost[i][j] = best
print(cost[0][n - 1])
